The ‘vanishing’ Seal Population

By: Mosibudi Ratlebjane | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a curious case of the Cape Towns dying, Seal Population: From allegations of animal cruelty, to overfishing and even a potential climate change crises, CB investigates just what exactly is behind t

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa’s marine scientists and conservationists have been baffled by a recent surge in seal deaths in Cape Town in 2021. As they continue to try to uncover what lies at the bottom of the mysterious happenings in our oceans, we take viewers on an unfolding journey of discovery on what might be a far bigger problem than dying seals.

Since the middle of 2021, beachgoers and scientists alike have been alarmed by the sheer number of seal carcasses washing up on various shores around Cape Town. But what exactly is going on, is it a natural phenomenon, or is there something more sinister at play?
Various worlds collide in this investigation into this mystery. Subsistence fishermen and suspected trawlers are often found in gruelling battles with seals to fight off food insecurity. Visual evidence seen by Carte Blanche shows the gruesome ending to these duels often play out at sea. Big foreign and local fishing trawlers also pose a big threat, not only directly to the seals but to their access to food.
While the government's own investigations into the deaths reveals that the seals have been dying due to malnutrition, independent studies show a far more concerning problem; the presence of domoic acid.
This neurotoxin is released by algae in the country’s oceans due to a change in water conditions which experts say is brought about by climate change. Something that if not dealt with, could mean the traumatic scenes of seal carcasses may become a far more frequent scenario.


Summary:
The problem is sadly not unique to South Africa. A study published in 2020 in America showed a domoic acid hotspot caused by a heatwave that blanketed the Pacific ocean between 2013-2015 had wreaked havoc on the marine ecosystem.
We chat to plankton expert Doctor Stephen Bates in Canada about what lessons South Africa can learn about potential harm our marine ecosystem might face if left untreated
While those who have been working on the ground with these seals for decades say more can be done to protect these fascinating ocean creatures from these existing threats, they believe a bigger potential environmental crisis brought on by climate change, animal cruelty at the hands of fishermen competing for fish, as well as an national forming transparent algae bloom are just some of the suspected reasons for the surge of animal deaths.
We go to speak to all the relevant parties and do some testing of our own to find out what lies behind this growing problem and how it will impact the future of SA’s oceans.


Further information:
The treatment:
While in a boat, we go to the well known islands that would otherwise be populated with thousands of seals. The numbers are low and our presenter narrates how many holiday goers, wildlife lovers, adore spectating the wondrous sea life as just one of Cape town's attractions. But the numbers are down, while one can still spot a few seals, the alarming rate of seals found dead, injured on the shorelines late last year called for drastic attention and called to find out what the real cause of death.
With Drone footage of the vast coasts, We take a trip towards the islands, and we take a deep dive down the sea with professional divers, where less frequently these days we would spot seals and other sea life.
Our fact finding mission will start at the coast where we will witness one of many days that Kim Krynauw spends on the Cape’s shore lines across the sea. She runs rehabilitation centre in Hout Bay, and over the last couple of years has dedicated her days rescuing and rehabilitating disdressed fur seal pups and yearlings, which are released back into the ocean.
While our viewers see her feeding and treating the pups and matured seals, she informs us about how the number of dead, injured, and at times botched seals started to pick in early September of 2021. Her organisation kept finding malnourished, others not not eating at all. While she gives a glimpse of the most recent rescues our views get a first hand look at ailing seals and how their struggles back to health.
Running her NPO surviving on charitable donations, just last week there were reports of cable theft in the bay,leaving her and the seals in the dark. She believes that part of problem is the over fishing, and food competition between the seals and the local fishermen that may lead to the seals unable to fend for themselves, as they rush towards fishing boats with the expectation of getting lucky and the Hout Bay Seals Rescue Centre would find seals decapitated, some with unexplained gunshot wounds. Part of a wildlife/sea life conservation and protection community that stretches throughout the Western, Eastern Coast, and parts of the Namibian Coast lines. The group had been sending countless emails to the government, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and Environment requesting assistance with monitoring the oceans and fishermen's boats.
This is when we swiftly meet Jaques Nel, while he feeds his rescued birds, in his home in Saint Helena Bay, on the West Coast. Nel is popularly known as somewhat of the local pariah, particularly, due to the countless battles he has fought with the governmental officials, about the protection of the environment and its wildlife. He vehemently believes that the officials are turning a blind eye and what he says is blatant negligence/incompetence of the officials from the deaprtment.
In his view different seal life, like wales, dolphins crabs and starfish started washing up sporadically on the shores, a few years ago, and the he witness the mass seal death in Saint Helena Bay when he tried to raise alarms, only for the government to be alerted when the popular beaches of like the like of Camps Bay were swamped with seals late last year.
Nel’s interview segways into some of the perceptions some fishermen have and the violent treatment towards seals.
This is when we meet, Our Anonymous Fisherman, We’ll call him Thembalihle*. Thembe has been one and off fishing on the oceans in medium to larger boats. He says while fishing for tuner, snoek over the years, can honestly be likened to pirate- like parades where the rules on land don't apply at sea. For example conflicts between fishermen and captains bringing out their guns over payment issues, or workers disgruntled about the working hours.
Thembalihle* Having witnessed some of the violence enacted on seals, seals being shot at, for swimming too close, scaring fish off. He claims that while he doesn't really condone these kinds of actions, he understands why some captains fishermen would do this. As one could earn between R10 - R15, a fish is caught, and have to count how many crew members are on board to share the catch.
While on a good day one boat depending on the size, could catch say 2-3 tons of Fish, if one seal is spotted could could really hamper on the catch the money earned for each fisherman and not even begin to cover the captain’s expenses. This is a real concern for many. Something that Jaues will inform inform us about Investigator Oupa Chaucke from the Department of Environmental Affairs, Traveled from pretoria to investigate the the fishermen killings of the Fish, but since then, no report on the report has been published or file, even after evidence of there being a need for inspector on sea to monitor and search the fishing boats for Guns.
Under the Marine Living Resources act: Cpt 5 No person shall, use, permit to be used, or attempt to use any explosive, fire-arm, poison or other noxious substance for the purpose of killing, stunning, disabling or catching fish, or of in any way rendering fish to be caught more easily;
Bus the actions from the Fishermen are not the only problem: As Cofounder of the scientific research organisation Sea Search, Doctor Tess Gridley, has been dealing with marine life her entire career.
She takes us to the two oceans aquarium in Cape Town where two seal carcusses have been preserved through freezing. She takes us through the process of extracting various samples of what she will be taking back to the laboratory with her for further testing by her team. This will give her further insights into two of the latest seals to have died. She also takes us through some of the common findings her and the team have discovered in dealing with this recent spate and what makes it different to what they’ve encountered before.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In a curious case of the Cape Towns dying, Seal Population: From allegations of animal cruelty, to overfishing and even a potential climate change crises, CB investigates just what exactly is behind t
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa’s marine scientists and conservationists have been baffled by a recent surge in seal deaths in Cape Town in 2021. As they continue to try to uncover what lies at the bottom of the mysterious happenings in our oceans, we take viewers on an unfolding journey of discovery on what might be a far bigger problem than dying seals. Since the middle of 2021, beachgoers and scientists alike have been alarmed by the sheer number of seal carcasses washing up on various shores around Cape Town. But what exactly is going on, is it a natural phenomenon, or is there something more sinister at play? Various worlds collide in this investigation into this mystery. Subsistence fishermen and suspected trawlers are often found in gruelling battles with seals to fight off food insecurity. Visual evidence seen by Carte Blanche shows the gruesome ending to these duels often play out at sea. Big foreign and local fishing trawlers also pose a big threat, not only directly to the seals but to their access to food. While the government's own investigations into the deaths reveals that the seals have been dying due to malnutrition, independent studies show a far more concerning problem; the presence of domoic acid. This neurotoxin is released by algae in the country’s oceans due to a change in water conditions which experts say is brought about by climate change. Something that if not dealt with, could mean the traumatic scenes of seal carcasses may become a far more frequent scenario.
metadata.Summary: The problem is sadly not unique to South Africa. A study published in 2020 in America showed a domoic acid hotspot caused by a heatwave that blanketed the Pacific ocean between 2013-2015 had wreaked havoc on the marine ecosystem. We chat to plankton expert Doctor Stephen Bates in Canada about what lessons South Africa can learn about potential harm our marine ecosystem might face if left untreated While those who have been working on the ground with these seals for decades say more can be done to protect these fascinating ocean creatures from these existing threats, they believe a bigger potential environmental crisis brought on by climate change, animal cruelty at the hands of fishermen competing for fish, as well as an national forming transparent algae bloom are just some of the suspected reasons for the surge of animal deaths. We go to speak to all the relevant parties and do some testing of our own to find out what lies behind this growing problem and how it will impact the future of SA’s oceans.
metadata.Further information: The treatment: While in a boat, we go to the well known islands that would otherwise be populated with thousands of seals. The numbers are low and our presenter narrates how many holiday goers, wildlife lovers, adore spectating the wondrous sea life as just one of Cape town's attractions. But the numbers are down, while one can still spot a few seals, the alarming rate of seals found dead, injured on the shorelines late last year called for drastic attention and called to find out what the real cause of death. With Drone footage of the vast coasts, We take a trip towards the islands, and we take a deep dive down the sea with professional divers, where less frequently these days we would spot seals and other sea life. Our fact finding mission will start at the coast where we will witness one of many days that Kim Krynauw spends on the Cape’s shore lines across the sea. She runs rehabilitation centre in Hout Bay, and over the last couple of years has dedicated her days rescuing and rehabilitating disdressed fur seal pups and yearlings, which are released back into the ocean. While our viewers see her feeding and treating the pups and matured seals, she informs us about how the number of dead, injured, and at times botched seals started to pick in early September of 2021. Her organisation kept finding malnourished, others not not eating at all. While she gives a glimpse of the most recent rescues our views get a first hand look at ailing seals and how their struggles back to health. Running her NPO surviving on charitable donations, just last week there were reports of cable theft in the bay,leaving her and the seals in the dark. She believes that part of problem is the over fishing, and food competition between the seals and the local fishermen that may lead to the seals unable to fend for themselves, as they rush towards fishing boats with the expectation of getting lucky and the Hout Bay Seals Rescue Centre would find seals decapitated, some with unexplained gunshot wounds. Part of a wildlife/sea life conservation and protection community that stretches throughout the Western, Eastern Coast, and parts of the Namibian Coast lines. The group had been sending countless emails to the government, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and Environment requesting assistance with monitoring the oceans and fishermen's boats. This is when we swiftly meet Jaques Nel, while he feeds his rescued birds, in his home in Saint Helena Bay, on the West Coast. Nel is popularly known as somewhat of the local pariah, particularly, due to the countless battles he has fought with the governmental officials, about the protection of the environment and its wildlife. He vehemently believes that the officials are turning a blind eye and what he says is blatant negligence/incompetence of the officials from the deaprtment. In his view different seal life, like wales, dolphins crabs and starfish started washing up sporadically on the shores, a few years ago, and the he witness the mass seal death in Saint Helena Bay when he tried to raise alarms, only for the government to be alerted when the popular beaches of like the like of Camps Bay were swamped with seals late last year. Nel’s interview segways into some of the perceptions some fishermen have and the violent treatment towards seals. This is when we meet, Our Anonymous Fisherman, We’ll call him Thembalihle*. Thembe has been one and off fishing on the oceans in medium to larger boats. He says while fishing for tuner, snoek over the years, can honestly be likened to pirate- like parades where the rules on land don't apply at sea. For example conflicts between fishermen and captains bringing out their guns over payment issues, or workers disgruntled about the working hours. Thembalihle* Having witnessed some of the violence enacted on seals, seals being shot at, for swimming too close, scaring fish off. He claims that while he doesn't really condone these kinds of actions, he understands why some captains fishermen would do this. As one could earn between R10 - R15, a fish is caught, and have to count how many crew members are on board to share the catch. While on a good day one boat depending on the size, could catch say 2-3 tons of Fish, if one seal is spotted could could really hamper on the catch the money earned for each fisherman and not even begin to cover the captain’s expenses. This is a real concern for many. Something that Jaues will inform inform us about Investigator Oupa Chaucke from the Department of Environmental Affairs, Traveled from pretoria to investigate the the fishermen killings of the Fish, but since then, no report on the report has been published or file, even after evidence of there being a need for inspector on sea to monitor and search the fishing boats for Guns. Under the Marine Living Resources act: Cpt 5 No person shall, use, permit to be used, or attempt to use any explosive, fire-arm, poison or other noxious substance for the purpose of killing, stunning, disabling or catching fish, or of in any way rendering fish to be caught more easily; Bus the actions from the Fishermen are not the only problem: As Cofounder of the scientific research organisation Sea Search, Doctor Tess Gridley, has been dealing with marine life her entire career. She takes us to the two oceans aquarium in Cape Town where two seal carcusses have been preserved through freezing. She takes us through the process of extracting various samples of what she will be taking back to the laboratory with her for further testing by her team. This will give her further insights into two of the latest seals to have died. She also takes us through some of the common findings her and the team have discovered in dealing with this recent spate and what makes it different to what they’ve encountered before.
